new_statements.quote: p. 77: "Um olhar sobre o padrão acentual em Taurepang revela a regularidade do padrão iâmbico. [...] Primeiro, deve-se considerar o padrão iâmbico, contando-se do início da palavra, da esquerda para direita, onde a segunda sílaba será acentuada. Nesta posição percebe-se com freqüência a ocorrência de sílabas pesadas. Por fim, a última sílaba, mesmo quando monomoráica, sempre é acentuada." p. 79: "Em Taurepang esta proeminência da sílaba final é categórica, ocorrendo independente do peso silábico e mesmo quando não se encontra na posição do padrão iâmbico, o que leva a assumir a seguinte regra geral de acento: a sílaba final sempre apresenta proeminência." p. 98: "- direção: da esquerda para a direita - padrão rítmico: iâmbico - sensibilidade ao peso silábico -ocorrência de pés degenerados - proibição de extrametricidade."
new_statements.translation: p. 77: "A look at the accentual pattern of Taurepang reveals the regularity of the iambic pattern. [...] First, one must consider the iambic pattern, counting from the beginning of the word, from left to right, where the second syllable will be stressed. In this position heavy syllables are frequently found. Finally, the last syllable, even when monomoraic, is always stressed." p. 79: "In Taurepang this prominence of the final syllable is categorical, occurring independently of syllable weight and even when it is not in the position of the iambic pattern, which leads one to assume the following general stress rule: the final syllable always shows prominence." p. 98: "- direction: from left to right - rhythmic pattern: iambic - sensitivity to syllable weight - occurrence of degenerate feet - prohibition of extrametricality."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records final stress for Pemon. Pessoa agrees that the final syllable is always prominent (categorical, weight-independent) and adds detail: a weight-sensitive iambic secondary rhythm from the left, degenerate final feet, no extrametricality, and a disyllable quirk (initial light syllable also prominent). Her remarks on Pemón proper are second-hand from Alvarez (1997): 'em Pemón são permitidos pés degenerados e.. a última sílaba apresenta proeminência' (p. 93), consistent with the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The final syllable of every word is always prominent (high pitch; a degenerate foot when light), regardless of weight or of the iambic count; in addition an iambic, weight-sensitive rhythm runs left to right from the first syllable, putting beats on even-numbered syllables (with iambic lengthening of the stressed light vowel) and on heavy syllables (long vowel or closed syllable) wherever they fall. Pessoa hypothesises two co-acting systems: the iambic rhythm and an autonomous final-syllable stress 'of equal importance'. She does not label one of them primary for Taurepang, but on p. 78 states that in Pemón (Alvarez 1997) and Ingarikó the final syllable is a degenerate foot 'que recebe acento primário' (that receives primary stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iambic rhythmic beats on the second, fourth.. syllables counting from the left (e.g. a.ri.ma.RAA.ka 'dog' with final prominence too); heavy syllables (CVV, CVC) attract prominence outside the rhythm; in disyllables the initial light syllable also carries high pitch and allophonic lengthening (both syllables prominent), a behaviour she says Alvarez 1997 does not discuss for Pemón (p. 93).
new_statements.exceptions: Initial-syllable prominence in disyllabic words (both syllables prominent) and on word-initial heavy syllables, after which the iambic count restarts; initial long vowels sometimes only surface (compensatory lengthening / vowel fusion). Analysis restricted to word level; author calls it preliminary ('não se pretende completa', fn. 14).
new_statements.identity_note: Pessoa 2006 describes Taurepang as spoken in the village of Boca da Mata, northern Roraima, Brazil (data from one main consultant). Glottolog treats Taurepan/Taulipang as a dialect of Pemon (pemo1248, ISO aoc), but the thesis itself lists Taurepang and Pemón as separate members of the Pemóng group and cites Alvarez (1997) for Pemón proper; its Pemón statements (final-syllable prominence, degenerate feet allowed) are therefore reported from Alvarez, not from the author's own data. Swiggers 2009 (Venezuelan Pemón) could not be opened.

All three are held and the quotations were verified at the stated places.
